ch9n1.title: Why is everyone packing?

questions.q: How do we know summer is ending, even though it is still warm and sunny?

options.text: Lots of birds have gone quiet or left, and more are flying south.
options.why: Clue: the cuckoo "had long been silent", other birds are "missing too", and the Rat hears wings passing at night with "a southing tendency".

options.text: Snow has started to fall on the river and the fields are turning white.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 1 says "light and warmth and colour were still present". No snow yet!

options.text: The Rat has to light a big fire every evening to keep himself warm.
options.why: Clue check: nobody lights a fire tonight. Look at what the birds are doing in paragraph 1.

options.text: birds flying off
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The storyteller says *Nature’s Grand Hotel has its Season, like the others.* What is the countryside being compared to?

options.text: A hotel where guests leave when the holiday ends, like the birds.
options.why: Clue: "the guests one by one pack, pay, and depart". The animals leaving for winter are like hotel guests going home.

options.text: A real hotel by the river where the animals all go on their holidays.
options.why: Clue check: nobody in the story visits a hotel. The storyteller is comparing the countryside to one.

options.text: A grand hotel that the Rat is about to open up in his house by the river.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 2 says the Rat "stayed" while others went. He isn't opening anything.

options.text: a holiday hotel
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How can we tell the field-mice are getting ready to move house?

options.text: They look at plans of flats and pack trunks and piles of food.
options.why: Clue: they "examined plans and drawings of small flats", hauled out "dusty trunks" and had food "ready for transport".

options.text: They tell the Rat they are all going on a boat trip down the river.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 8 the field-mouse says "I think not to-day" when the Rat suggests a row.

options.text: They build a big new house of wheat right in the middle of the field.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 6 says they must move out "before those horrid machines begin clicking round the fields". They are leaving the field.

options.text: having a picnic
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: in paragraph 3 the food is piled up "ready for transport", not for eating.

questions.q: A field-mouse explains *rather shamefacedly*. How is the field-mouse feeling?

options.text: A bit embarrassed, because they know it's much too early to pack.
options.why: Clue: the field-mouse says "Of course, we're early, we know that". Shamefaced means a bit embarrassed.

options.text: Their face is all dirty from digging, so they try to hide it away.
options.why: Clue check: shamefaced is about a feeling, not a dirty face. What does the field-mouse admit in paragraph 6?

options.text: Very proud of how early they have started their packing this year.
options.why: Clue check: the field-mouse says "we're only just making a start", almost saying sorry. That's not proud.

options.text: a bit embarrassed
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: What makes a field-mouse tell the Rat he had better sit down somewhere?

options.text: He trips over a hat-box and gets in the way of their packing.
options.why: Clue: he "tripped over a hat-box, and fell", and the mouse says "If people would be more careful... and look where they're going".

options.text: He starts eating their nuts and barley without asking them first.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat doesn't eat anything. Look at what he falls over in paragraph 9.

options.text: He climbs into their new flat and refuses to come back out again.
options.why: Clue check: the flats are only "plans and drawings". Nobody has moved in yet.

options.text: he ate nuts
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 9 says what the Rat did, and it's clumsy, not greedy.

questions.q: At first the Rat asks the field-mice to come for a row or a picnic. How has his mood changed by the time he leaves the field?

options.text: He is grumpy and fed up, as nobody has time for him.
options.why: Clue: he says "You won't be 'free'... this side of Christmas" and leaves "grumpily".

options.text: He is happy, as the mice have promised to picnic with him later on.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 8 the mouse only says "Perhaps some other day". That's not a promise.

options.text: He is excited, as he has decided to move into a little new flat too.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 12 says he goes back to his river, which "never packed up". He isn't moving.

options.text: sleepy and bored
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: look at the word in paragraph 11 that says how the Rat answers.

questions.q: The Rat goes back to *his faithful, steady-going old river, which never packed up*. Why does he like the river so much today?

options.text: It stays put, unlike his friends who are packing up.
options.why: Clue: the river "never packed up, flitted, or went into winter quarters", unlike the mice and the birds.

options.text: The river has never owned a suitcase, so it can't go on holiday.
options.why: Clue check: rivers don't pack! The storyteller is comparing the river to the animals who are leaving.

options.text: The river is his old pet, and it follows him wherever he goes.
options.why: Clue check: steady-going means it stays the same and stays put. It doesn't follow anyone.

options.text: always stays put
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Rat thinks leaving must make the swallows sad. What does a swallow say later that shows they feel the opposite?

options.text: They feel a sweet unrest, as memories of far places call them.
options.why: Clue: "we feel it stirring within us, a sweet unrest" and the names of "long-forgotten places come gradually back and beckon to us".

options.text: They say they hate flying and wish they could stay by the river.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 15 a swallow says planning the trip is "half the fun".

options.text: They say they are only leaving because the Rat was rude to them.
options.why: Clue check: the swallows were planning before the Rat even arrived, in paragraph 13.

options.text: the Rat was rude
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: read how the second swallow describes the feeling in paragraph 17.

questions.q: Which word best describes the Rat in tonight's passage, and what is your proof?

options.text: Unsettled: he can't settle to anything, with everyone leaving.
options.why: Clue: "It was difficult to settle down to anything seriously, with all this flitting going on."

options.text: Busy: he spends all day helping the field-mice pack their trunks.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 7 he says "O, bother starts" and asks them to come and play instead.

options.text: Brave: he flies off south with the swallows to see where they go.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat can't fly! In paragraph 12 he goes back to his river.

options.text: Cheerful: he waves the field-mice off and wishes them all good luck.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 9 he leaves "with a snort of contempt". That isn't cheerful.

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Rat feeling?

options.text: By the river, puzzled by the swallows' talk of far places.
options.why: Clue: the swallow tells him "No, you don't understand, naturally", then describes places that "beckon to us".

options.text: In the wheat field, happily helping the mice carry their bags.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat left the field back in paragraph 11. Where is he in the last paragraphs?

options.text: Asleep in his bed, dreaming of the swallows flying off south.
options.why: Clue check: at the end he is wide awake, talking to the swallows in the osiers.

options.text: happy and calm
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: in paragraph 16 the Rat says "that's just what I don't understand".

hints: The Rat begs the swallows to stay, but one says staying once nearly froze it, so it never will again.
The Rat feels lonely, so he rows off to find the Mole and they talk until the sun goes down.
The swallows leave early, but a storm blows them back, so they stay with the Rat all winter.
The Rat can't stop thinking about the South, but a tired stranger sits down and tells him all about it.

ch9n2.title: A stranger on the road

questions.q: Why did one swallow give up trying to stay behind for the winter?

options.text: The nights were long and cold, and there were no insects to eat.
options.why: Clue: "O the weary length of the nights! The shivering, sunless days!" and "not an insect in an acre of it!"

options.text: The other swallows flew back and made it fly south with all of them.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 2 the swallow says "I took wing" by itself, one stormy night.

options.text: The Rat asked it to go away because it kept him awake at night.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat wants the swallows to stay! Look at his question in paragraph 1.

options.text: too cold and hungry
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The swallow says *The past was like a bad dream*. What does the swallow mean?

options.text: Once it was warm in the South, the cold felt far away.
options.why: Clue: it came after "the hot sun again on my back" and "the future was all happy holiday". The cold was over, like waking from a bad dream.

options.text: The swallow fell fast asleep and dreamed about being cold.
options.why: Clue check: the cold really happened. The swallow says it was "like" a dream, not that it was one.

options.text: The swallow had nightmares every night in the warm South.
options.why: Clue check: in the South the swallow was "easily, lazily, lingering". That sounds happy, not scary.

options.text: it was sleeping
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: the word "like" tells you it's a comparison, not real sleep.

questions.q: How do we know the swallows' talk has changed how the Rat sees his own home?

options.text: When he opens his eyes, the river looks chill and the fields grey.
options.why: Clue: "when he looked again the river seemed steely and chill, the green fields grey and lightless".

options.text: He says his river is the best place in the world and always will be.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 4 he calls it "this poor drab little country".

options.text: He decides to paint his house in the bright colours of the South.
options.why: Clue check: nobody paints anything. Look at what happens when he opens his eyes in paragraph 3.

options.text: home looks dull
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: *Then his loyal heart seemed to cry out on his weaker self for its treachery.* Why does the Rat feel this?

options.text: Part of him feels guilty for dreaming of leaving his river.
options.why: Clue: he has just been dreaming of "the real southern sun". His loyal heart loves the river, so the dream feels like a betrayal.

options.text: His heart is sore because he ran up the hill much too fast.
options.why: Clue check: he has been lying still "with closed eyes". This is about feelings, not running.

options.text: He told the swallows a lie, and his heart is cross about it.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat hasn't told any lies. What was he just dreaming about in paragraph 3?

options.text: feels guilty
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Rat asks why the swallows ever come back. What do they say that shows they miss this place too?

options.text: In spring they long for meadows, ponds and water-lilies.
options.why: Clue: they speak of "lush meadow-grass... warm, insect-haunted ponds" and being "home-sick once more for quiet water-lilies".

options.text: They say they only come back because the Rat gives them food.
options.why: Clue check: the swallows never mention the Rat feeding them. Read paragraphs 5 to 7.

options.text: They say they come back to see the robin, their best friend.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 6 mentions the cuckoo, not the robin, and nobody is called a best friend.

options.text: they like robins
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: look at what the third swallow is home-sick for in paragraph 7.

questions.q: How can we tell the Rat is kind to the tired stranger when he first arrives?

options.text: He lets him rest quietly and doesn't pester him with questions.
options.why: Clue: "the Rat let him rest unquestioned", knowing the value of "mere silent companionship".

options.text: He runs home at once to fetch him a big bowl of hot soup to eat.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat stays sitting beside him in paragraph 11. Nobody fetches food tonight.

options.text: He gives the stranger his own warm jersey to put on over his.
options.why: Clue check: the jersey in paragraph 12 is the stranger's own, "of a faded blue".

options.text: fetches soup
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: the kindness in paragraph 11 is about being quiet, not food.

questions.q: The Rat agrees *without his usual whole-hearted conviction*. Does he really believe his life is the only life?

options.text: Not quite; he says so, but now he isn't so sure any more.
options.why: Clue: he answers "dreamily", and without his usual whole-hearted conviction, which means he isn't as sure as he used to be.

options.text: Yes, he is sure, and his whole heart is shouting it out loud.
options.why: Clue check: the quote says "without" his whole heart. That's the opposite of sure.

options.text: No, he hates the river and has always wanted to leave it.
options.why: Clue check: earlier he loved his "faithful" river. He is only starting to wonder, not hating it.

options.text: not so sure
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The stranger says the Rat's life is the best in the world. So why is he walking away from that same kind of life?

options.text: He tried it for six months, but the old call of the South won.
options.why: Clue: "six months of it" and now he is "tramping southward, following the old call, back to the old life".

options.text: The farm he lived on burned down, so he had nowhere left to live.
options.why: Clue check: nobody mentions a fire. He says he is following "the old call".

options.text: The farmer sent him away for being lazy and eating all the crops.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 16 he chose to go. Nobody sent him.

options.text: the old call
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Which word best describes the stranger when he first arrives, and what is your proof?

options.text: Weary: he walks slowly, sits down and rests before he speaks.
options.why: Clue: he "walked somewhat wearily", "seemed tired", and only spoke "When he had rested awhile".

options.text: Rude: he pushes past the Rat without even saying hello to him.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 11 says he "saluted with a gesture of courtesy" and smiled.

options.text: Grumpy: he tells the Rat the countryside here is dull and horrid.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 14 he calls it "a goodly life", "no doubt the best in the world".

options.text: Lively: he skips up the lane, bouncing along and full of energy.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 16 says he is "footsore and hungry". No skipping!

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Rat feeling?

options.text: By the lane, dreading that the stranger is heading South too.
options.why: Clue: "Is this, then, yet another of them?" He "hardly dared to ask where he was bound for", as he already knew.

options.text: At home by his fire, glad that the swallows have all flown away.
options.why: Clue check: at the end he is lying by the dusty lane with the stranger, not at home.

options.text: On a ship with the stranger, excited to sail away to the South.
options.why: Clue check: nobody is on a ship. They are sitting in the grass by the road.

options.text: fast asleep
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: in the last paragraph the Rat is asking the stranger questions.

hints: The stranger is a sailor who got bored of farming, so he tells the Rat all about his voyages.
The stranger is hungry but too proud to ask, so the Rat pretends he has far too much food.
The stranger is lost, so the Rat draws him a map until he can find the right road.
The stranger's feet are sore, but the Rat rows him down the river so he can rest them.

ch9n3.title: Tales of the sea

questions.q: How do we know the stranger is not sorry to have left his farm?

options.text: He says he's glad to be here, many miles nearer his heart's desire.
options.why: Clue: "Glad to be here all the same, though, glad to be here! So many miles further on the road".

options.text: He cries about his lovely farm and says he'll go back there tomorrow.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 1 he says "Never mind about it". He doesn't want to talk about the farm.

options.text: He says the farm was horrid and he never once had enough to eat.
options.why: Clue check: he says "I had everything I could want" at the farm.

options.text: glad he left
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: *His shining eyes held fast to the horizon*. What does this tell us about the stranger?

options.text: He keeps staring far away, longing to be somewhere else.
options.why: Clue: he seems to be "listening for some sound that was wanting", something missing from the farmland around him.

options.text: His eyes are stuck, so he can't stop looking at the sky.
options.why: Clue check: held fast is about wanting to keep looking, not being stuck. He isn't hurt.

options.text: His eyes are shining because he has something caught in them.
options.why: Clue check: shining eyes here are eager eyes. Look at what he is listening for in paragraph 2.

options.text: longing to go
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Why does the Sea Rat feel at home in so many different ports?

options.text: He has sailed to all of them, so everybody there knows him.
options.why: Clue: "I know them all, and they know me. Set me down on any of their quays... and I am home again."

options.text: He owns a little house in every port, full of his own things.
options.why: Clue check: he never talks about owning houses. It's the people he knows that make him feel at home.

options.text: His family lives in every single port and always lets him stay.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 4 he says even the city of his birth "is no more my home" than any other port.

options.text: owns many houses
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: read the last two sentences of paragraph 4.

questions.q: The Water Rat imagines the Sea Rat far out at sea for months. What does the Sea Rat say that shows he isn't like that?

options.text: He stays near the coast and loves the fun on shore just as much.
options.why: Clue: "I'm in the coasting trade, and rarely out of sight of land. It's the jolly times on shore that appeal to me."

options.text: He says he gets seasick, so he only ever sails on little rivers.
options.why: Clue check: nobody gets seasick. He sails round the seas of the South, just close to land.

options.text: He says he has never been on a ship and walks everywhere instead.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 8 he says "I shipped myself on board a small trading vessel".

options.text: gets seasick
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 6 says what kind of sailing he likes.

questions.q: The Water Rat says *my life, I confess to you, feels to me to-day somewhat narrow and circumscribed*. What does he mean?

options.text: His own life feels small and dull next to the stranger's.
options.why: Clue: he wants to hear about coasting to "warm his latter days with gallant memories". Narrow means small, with not much in it.

options.text: His house by the river has got too thin for him to fit inside it.
options.why: Clue check: he says his life feels narrow, not his house. This is about feelings.

options.text: He has been tied up with string, so he can't move very far away.
options.why: Clue check: nobody is tied up! He is sitting in the grass listening.

options.text: life feels small
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Sea Rat says *The domestic storm-cone was hoisted*. What does he mean?

options.text: There was trouble at home, so he went off to sea again.
options.why: Clue: the sentence before says "Family troubles, as usual, began it." A storm-cone is a warning signal that a storm is coming.

options.text: A huge storm hit his house, so he climbed up a tall cone.
options.why: Clue check: domestic means at home, with family. The storm here is a family row, not weather.

options.text: His family all sailed away on a ship with a cone-shaped sail.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 8 he says "I shipped myself". He went, not his family.

options.text: family trouble
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How can we tell the Water Rat is carried away by the story about Venice?

options.text: He goes silent and dreams he is floating along the canals.
options.why: Clue: "the Water Rat, silent too and enthralled, floated on dream-canals".

options.text: He jumps up and starts packing his bag to go to Venice now.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 9 he doesn't move at all. He just sits and dreams.

options.text: He interrupts to say that Venice sounds much too noisy for him.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 9 says he was "silent". He doesn't interrupt.

options.text: he claps
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: find the word "enthralled" in paragraph 9. What is he doing?

questions.q: The Water Rat thinks life on a ship must be hot and hard. How do the Sea Rat's winks show it isn't hard for him?

options.text: He sleeps in the captain's cabin; it's only hard for the crew.
options.why: Clue: "The captain's cabin's good enough for me" and "For the crew it is", both said with a wink.

options.text: He works harder than any sailor and never gets a wink of sleep.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 10 he spent "many jolly weeks" resting on shore. Not very hard work!

options.text: He winks because he has got some sea-spray stuck in his eye.
options.why: Clue check: a wink here is a joke. He is hinting that he has an easy time.

options.text: a comfy cabin
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Which word best describes the Sea Rat, and what is your proof?

options.text: Adventurous: he never sticks too long to one ship or place.
options.why: Clue: "I never stick too long to one ship", and he moves from Venice to Sicily to Corsica and on.

options.text: Shy: he won't tell the Water Rat anything at all about his travels.
options.why: Clue check: he talks and talks about his voyages all through this passage.

options.text: Homesick: he talks all the time about missing his farm up north.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 1 he says "Never mind about it" when talking about his farm.

options.text: Hard-working: he always sleeps down in the hold with the crew.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 12 he says "The captain's cabin's good enough for me."

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Sea Rat feeling?

options.text: Still telling tales, missing Marseilles so much he dreams of it.
options.why: Clue: "sometimes I dream of the shell-fish of Marseilles, and wake up crying!" He misses it that much.

options.text: Asleep in the grass, tired out after the long walk from his farm.
options.why: Clue check: in the last paragraph he is still talking.

options.text: On a ship in Marseilles, eating a huge dinner of fresh shell-fish.
options.why: Clue check: he is only remembering Marseilles. He is still sitting by the road with the Water Rat.

options.text: bored and grumpy
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: someone who dreams of a place and wakes up crying is missing it.

hints: The Sea Rat is starving, so the Water Rat fetches a picnic for them to share by the road.
The Sea Rat falls asleep in the middle of a story, so the Water Rat waits until he wakes.
The Mole comes looking for Ratty, but the stories keep them both listening until dark.
The Water Rat longs to see the sea, but it's too far, so the Sea Rat draws it in the dust.

ch9n4.title: A picnic by the road

questions.q: Why does the Sea Rat want to eat outside instead of going into the Water Rat's home?

options.text: Indoors he'd fall asleep, but outside he can tell stories.
options.why: Clue: "while we eat, I could tell you more concerning my voyages" but "if we go indoors... I shall presently fall asleep".

options.text: He is scared of the Water Rat's home because it is dark inside.
options.why: Clue check: he never says he's scared. Read his two reasons at the end of paragraph 2.

options.text: He has muddy boots and doesn't want to spoil the Rat's carpets.
options.why: Clue check: nobody mentions boots or carpets. What does he say would happen indoors?

options.text: muddy boots
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 2 says what would happen "if we go indoors".

questions.q: The Sea Rat says *I am none too fond of going under hatches*. What does he mean?

options.text: He doesn't like going indoors, like sailors going below deck.
options.why: Clue: he asks "couldn't you fetch it along out here?" Hatches are the doors down into a ship. He is talking like a sailor.

options.text: He doesn't like hens hatching eggs, as they make too much noise.
options.why: Clue check: nobody mentions hens. He is answering an invitation to go into the Rat's hole.

options.text: He is scared of trapdoors and thinks he might fall through one.
options.why: Clue check: none too fond means he doesn't like it much. It's not about falling.

options.text: prefers outdoors
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How do we know the Water Rat thinks hard about what his guest would like to eat?

options.text: He packs French bread and garlic sausage, food from the South.
options.why: Clue: "remembering the stranger's origin and preferences, he took care to include a yard of long French bread, a sausage out of which the garlic sang".

options.text: He asks the Sea Rat to write a list of all the foods he likes best.
options.why: Clue check: the Water Rat "hurried off home" without asking. He remembered by himself.

options.text: He bakes a big fish pie, because all sailors love eating fish.
options.why: Clue check: there's no pie in the basket. Look at the list of food in paragraph 3.

options.text: a fish pie
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 3 lists what went in the basket. Is there a pie?

questions.q: The Rat packs *some cheese which lay down and cried*. Does the cheese really cry?

options.text: No, it's so soft and ripe that it runs, as if it's crying.
options.why: Clue: the garlic "sang" and the cheese "cried". The storyteller is having fun making food sound alive. A very ripe cheese goes runny.

options.text: Yes, it is a sad cheese that cried when it went in the basket.
options.why: Clue check: cheese can't be sad! The garlic sausage "sang" in the same sentence. It's a funny way of describing food.

options.text: Yes, it's wet because the Rat dropped it in the river on the way.
options.why: Clue check: nobody drops anything. The Rat "returned with all speed" and they unpacked it happily.

options.text: runny ripe cheese
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Sea Rat's story ends at his quiet inland farm. How does the Water Rat feel about that part?

options.text: He finds the farm dull and only wants to hear about the sea.
options.why: Clue: he left the Sea Rat "with a regretful sigh planted at his dull inland farm, about which he desired to hear nothing".

options.text: He is glad the Sea Rat has found somewhere quiet to live at last.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 5 says "a regretful sigh". That's not glad.

options.text: He asks lots of questions about all the cows and crops on the farm.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 5 says he "desired to hear nothing" about the farm.

options.text: farm is dull
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: *The twin lights, the shifting grey and the steadfast red, mastered the Water Rat and held him bound*. What has happened to the Water Rat?

options.text: He is so spellbound by the Sea Rat that he can't look away.
options.why: Clue: the same sentence says "fascinated, powerless". The Sea Rat's grey eyes hold him like a spell.

options.text: The Sea Rat has tied him up with rope after they finished lunch.
options.why: Clue check: held him bound is about a spell, not rope. Nobody gets tied up.

options.text: He is looking at two lamps shining red and grey along the road.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 6 says the grey is the Sea Rat's eyes. The "lights" are not lamps.

options.text: under a spell
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How can we tell the Water Rat has forgotten everything around him while the Sea Rat talks?

options.text: The quiet world around them seems to fade away to nothing.
options.why: Clue: "The quiet world outside their rays receded far away and ceased to be."

options.text: He forgets his own name and has to ask the Sea Rat what it is.
options.why: Clue check: nobody forgets a name. Look for what "receded far away" in paragraph 6.

options.text: He forgets to eat, so his lunch is left untouched on the grass.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 6 begins "By this time their meal was over". They had already eaten.

options.text: stops listening
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: he listens harder than ever. It's everything else he forgets.

questions.q: Earlier the Sea Rat was heading for a quiet farm. At the end, where does he say he is going now?

options.text: To a little grey sea town, to catch a ship sailing South.
options.why: Clue: "I take to the road again... till at last I reach the little grey sea town", and the ship ends "pointing South!"

options.text: Back to his inland farm, to settle down there for good this time.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 5 says he left the farm. Now he talks about a harbour and a ship.

options.text: Home with the Water Rat, to live beside his river for ever.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 8 he says "I take to the road again".

options.text: back to sea
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Which word best describes the Water Rat in this passage, and what is your proof?

options.text: Generous: he fetches lunch for a hungry stranger he just met.
options.why: Clue: "you are very welcome to whatever there is", and he hurries home to pack a basket for them both.

options.text: Mean: he eats all the lunch himself and gives the stranger crumbs.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 3 "together they unpacked the basket" and shared it.

options.text: Bored: he yawns and wanders off in the middle of the Sea Rat's tale.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 5 says he was "Spell-bound and quivering with excitement".

options.text: Rude: he tells the Sea Rat to stop talking and go away at once.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 1 calls him "the polite Water Rat".

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Water Rat feeling?

options.text: Still by the road, spellbound as the Sea Rat talks of sailing.
options.why: Clue: the Sea Rat is "still holding him fast with his sea-grey eyes" while he describes the voyage South.

options.text: Back at home, glad the Sea Rat has gone and all is quiet again.
options.why: Clue check: in the last paragraph the Sea Rat is still talking to him.

options.text: On a ship's deck, feeling seasick as the green waves slap the sides.
options.why: Clue check: the ship is only in the Sea Rat's story. The Water Rat hasn't moved from the roadside.

options.text: bored stiff
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: paragraph 7 says the Sea Rat is "still holding him fast".

hints: The Rat packs a bag to follow the Sea Rat, but the Mole grabs him at the door and holds him back.
The Sea Rat misses his ship, so he stays with the Water Rat until the next spring.
The Rat longs to go South, but the Mole gets him writing poems until he feels better.
The Sea Rat leaves his map behind, so the Water Rat runs after him until he catches up.

ch9n5.title: The call of the South

questions.q: The Sea Rat says *'Tis but a banging of the door behind you*. What is he telling the Water Rat?

options.text: Leaving is easy: just shut the door behind you and go.
options.why: Clue: he goes on "a blithesome step forward, and you are out of the old life and into the new!" He makes leaving sound simple.

options.text: The Rat must bang his front door hard enough to break it.
options.why: Clue check: nobody wants the door broken. The Sea Rat means it only takes one small step to leave.

options.text: The Sea Rat is angry and wants the Water Rat to slam the door.
options.why: Clue check: the Sea Rat is kind, calling him "young brother". He isn't angry.

options.text: just go
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: How do we know the Rat is not really himself as he gets ready to leave?

options.text: He moves about slowly like a sleep-walker, with lips parted.
options.why: Clue: "Mechanically" twice, "moving about the room like a sleep-walker; listening ever with parted lips".

options.text: He runs around shouting and knocking over all of his furniture.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 3 says "carefully and without haste". He is slow and quiet.

options.text: He writes the Mole a long letter to say goodbye properly.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 5 he doesn't even look at the Mole. No letter!

options.text: very excited
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: find the word "sleep-walker" in paragraph 3.

questions.q: The Rat leaves *with no haste, but with no hesitation at all*. What does that show?

options.text: He isn't rushing, but nothing will change his mind about it.
options.why: Clue: no haste means not hurrying, and no hesitation means not stopping to wonder. In paragraph 6 he goes on "with dogged fixity of purpose".

options.text: He is walking very fast and bumping into everything he sees.
options.why: Clue check: no haste means he is NOT hurrying. He moves slowly.

options.text: He can't decide whether to go, so he keeps stopping and starting.
options.why: Clue check: no hesitation means he doesn't stop at all. He has decided.

options.text: slow but sure
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Why does the Mole drag the Rat back inside?

options.text: The Rat's eyes look like another animal's, so Mole is scared.
options.why: Clue: the Mole, "now thoroughly alarmed", sees the eyes are "not his friend's eyes, but the eyes of some other animal!"

options.text: The Mole wants the Rat to help him finish all the washing-up.
options.why: Clue check: paragraph 6 says the Mole is "thoroughly alarmed". This is serious, not chores.

options.text: The Mole wants to go South too and needs to borrow the satchel.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 7 the Mole locks the satchel away. He doesn't want it.

options.text: the Rat was rude
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: look into the Rat's eyes with the Mole in paragraph 6.

questions.q: How does the Mole make sure the Rat can't just walk off again?

options.text: He fastens the door and locks the Rat's satchel in a drawer.
options.why: Clue: "Mole made the door fast, threw the satchel into a drawer and locked it".

options.text: He ties the Rat to his chair with a long bit of washing-line.
options.why: Clue check: nobody is tied up. Look at what the Mole does with the door and the satchel.

options.text: He hides the Rat's stick up the chimney where no one can find it.
options.why: Clue check: the stick isn't mentioned again. Find what the Mole locks away in paragraph 7.

options.text: sits on him
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: the Mole sits on the table, not on the Rat. What does he lock?

questions.q: When the Mole stops him, the Rat's eyes are grey and strange. How does the Mole know later that his friend is better?

options.text: His eyes are clear and dark and brown again, like before.
options.why: Clue: the Mole "took one hasty glance at his eyes; found them... clear and dark and brown again as before".

options.text: The Rat laughs and says he never wanted to go anywhere at all.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 8 the Rat is "listless, silent, and dejected". No laughing.

options.text: The Rat's eyes turn bright red, just like the colour of the South.
options.why: Clue check: read paragraph 8 again. What colour are his eyes when the Mole checks?

options.text: eyes are brown
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Sea Rat talked about the hot South. What does the Mole talk about to bring the Rat back to himself?

options.text: Harvest, apples and cosy winter at home, all right here.
options.why: Clue: he talks of "the harvest", "the reddening apples", jams, and midwinter's "snug home life".

options.text: Hot beaches and big ships, so the Rat can enjoy his dream more.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole wants to cure the Rat, not make the dream stronger. Look at paragraph 11.

options.text: The Wild Wood, to scare the Rat into staying safely indoors.
options.why: Clue check: the Wild Wood isn't mentioned at all tonight.

options.text: cosy home things
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: The Mole talks *Casually, then, and with seeming indifference*. Does the Mole really not care?

options.text: He cares a lot, but he pretends so the Rat won't notice.
options.why: Clue: seeming means it only looks that way. In paragraph 8 the Mole is "Very anxious in mind".

options.text: He really doesn't care, and is just chatting to pass the time.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole held the Rat back and watched over him all day. He cares a lot!

options.text: He is much too sleepy to care about what the Rat is feeling.
options.why: Clue check: nobody says the Mole is sleepy. He is busy trying to cheer his friend up.

options.text: only pretending
options.why: Right idea! Now make it a full sentence. Which option says it properly?

questions.q: Which word best describes how the Mole treats the Rat tonight, and what is your proof?

options.text: Tactful: he quietly leaves paper and a pencil to cheer him up.
options.why: Clue: "the tactful Mole slipped away and returned with a pencil and a few half-sheets of paper".

options.text: Unkind: he laughs at the Rat for wanting to go off to the South.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole never laughs at him. He is "Very anxious in mind".

options.text: Lazy: he goes off to bed and leaves the Rat all alone and sad.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 7 the Mole "sat down quietly on the table by his friend, waiting".

options.text: Bossy: he makes the Rat write a whole book of poems before bed.
options.why: Clue check: in paragraph 14 the Mole says "if it's only just the rhymes". That's gentle, not bossy.

questions.q: Where does tonight's bit of the story end, and how is the Mole feeling?

options.text: Peeping at the Rat scribbling, full of joy he's better.
options.why: Clue: the Rat is "alternately scribbling and sucking the top of his pencil", and "it was joy to the Mole to know that the cure had at least begun".

options.text: Waving the Rat off down the road, sad that he is going South.
options.why: Clue check: the Rat never leaves. The Mole stopped him in paragraph 6.

options.text: Packing his own bag, excited to go South with the Sea Rat.
options.why: Clue check: the Mole wants everyone to stay home. He talks about "snug home life" in paragraph 11.

options.text: very worried
options.why: That isn't a full sentence, and the idea slips past too. Clue check: he was worried earlier, but look at the very last word about the Mole in paragraph 15.

hints: Toad is lost and hungry after his escape, but a barge-woman offers him a ride along the canal.
The Rat still longs for the sea, so the Mole plans a boat trip down the river until he feels at home.
The Sea Rat comes back to fetch the Rat, but the Mole hides him in the cellar until he goes away.
Toad is still locked in his prison cell, so his friends dig a tunnel until they reach him.
